summary:
PetaniPal is a multilingual, voice-first app that helps Malaysian farmers compare crop-rotation options under uncertain weather. We built a prototype for one locality that listens to a farmer’s spoken field knowledge, such as past crops, flooding, irrigation and priorities. It reads each fact back for confirmation before saving it to the farmer’s private Farm Memory record.

The app addresses the challenge by combining that knowledge with NASA POWER daily climate history and local soil context. Our backend code calculates dry spells, heavy-rain days, heat stress and crop-season conditions. It then compares the farmer’s current rotation against two alternatives. An LLM only handles the conversation and explains the verified results in simple English or Bahasa Malaysia. Every answer states its evidence and what is still unknown.

This matters because climate variability makes planting decisions harder, and much of the most useful knowledge sits in farmers’ memories rather than in weather dashboards. PetaniPal turns that knowledge and open NASA data into clear, explainable decision support. It does not promise yields or replace agricultural experts, and it stores no raw voice recordings.
details:
What it does and how it works

***Just click SignIn to login and access the app***
PetaniPal is a voice-first app that helps farmers compare crop-rotation options. A farmer talks to it in English or Bahasa Malaysia and answers simple questions about the field. These cover what was planted last season, whether water stays on the field after heavy rain, whether irrigation is available, and what matters most for the next crop. The app reads important answers back for confirmation and saves only approved facts to the farmer’s private Farm Memory record.

The backend then gets NASA POWER daily climate history for the locality and adds local soil context from GeoTanih. Normal code, not the LLM, calculates dry spells, heavy-rain days, heat stress, and crop-season rainfall. A rule-based engine compares the farmer’s current rotation with two alternatives. For each option it shows climate and water fit, soil benefit, risks, missing information, and what the farmer should check. The LLM only understands the farmer’s speech, asks the next question, and explains the verified results in plain language. The farmer can also ask open questions at any time, such as “What if the rain starts late?”

Benefits

  • Farmers speak naturally and don’t need technical terms or reading skills.
  • It captures local knowledge that weather dashboards miss, such as which corner floods.
  • Every answer shows its evidence and what is unknown, using the labels Verified by farmer, Estimated from map or climate data, and Unknown.
  • It supports the farmer’s decision without telling them what to plant.

Intended impact

The goal is to help smallholder farmers plan rotations that hold up better under shifting rainfall, heat, and flood risk. It also builds a consented record of farm history that could later support better local models. The prototype covers one locality and four to six crops so the results are credible.

Tools and technology

  • Data: NASA POWER (daily climate), GeoTanih (Malaysian soil suitability), a hand-built crop library from Department of Agriculture and MARDI guidance, and dated FAMA price snapshots.
  • AI: speech-to-text and an LLM (OpenAI API in the current plan) for conversation, and text-to-speech to read answers aloud. The API key stays on the backend.
  • Interface: a mobile-style UI with a large voice button, a read-aloud text box, a language dropdown, an FAQ button, and Pal, Records, and Settings tabs.
  • Languages, frameworks, hosting, hardware: [fill in, e.g. Python backend, frontend framework, database, test devices].

What is creative about it

  • Farmers’ own observations come first. Farmers describe what they see, and the app converts it into structured values behind the scenes.
  • A clear split of roles: code does the calculations and the LLM does the talking. The LLM never invents crop facts or changes scores.
  • It shows evidence coverage (low, medium, or high) rather than a fake accuracy percentage.
  • Spoken “what if” scenarios replay historical dry, wet, or hot periods and say plainly that they are scenarios, not forecasts.
  • No raw voice is stored. The app keeps only the facts the farmer approves.

Factors the team considered

  • Honest limits: no yield prediction, because NASA data has no farm-outcome labels. ML is left for later, once consented outcome data exists.
  • Safety: diagnosis, chemical use, and other high-stakes questions are redirected to local agricultural officers.
  • Privacy: a precise promise about voice data, with on-device speech-to-text as the strongest option, and farmer control to review, correct, export, and delete records.
  • Data reliability: official sources with source URLs and review dates, and no live scraping.
  • Scope and language: one locality, with Bahasa Malaysia phrasing checked by fluent speakers.
  • Testing: checking calculations against NASA POWER and replaying known seasons.
